title: Delivery approaches: linear-sequential, iterative-incremental and hybrid
blurb: Define the three delivery approaches, say when each suits the work, and explain how PRINCE2 governs all of them.
question: A project will build a warehouse to a fixed design and develop its stock-control software in short increments based on user feedback. Which delivery approach is this, and does PRINCE2 need to change its principles to govern it?

teach.body: A delivery approach is the way the specialist work of producing the products is organized. PRINCE2 7 recognizes three: linear-sequential (one step after another, with products defined in detail up front), iterative-incremental (products evolve through repeated cycles) and hybrid (a mix of the two). PRINCE2 is not tied to any of them: it governs the project whichever approach the teams use.

teach.caption: Product descriptions are detailed enough to estimate cost and time with confidence before building.
Quality and acceptance criteria are refined in parallel with development, using a product backlog.
The building is linear-sequential; the software is iterative-incremental.

teach.body: PRINCE2 is not specific to any lifecycle or delivery method. Whatever the approach, all seven principles apply and the project still has at least two management stages: initiation plus one or more delivery stages. A simple project with few well-understood products may need only those two. An iterative project may have several delivery stages, each delivering increments from a product backlog. The method is tailored; the principles are not.

root.label: How well understood are the products?

teach.body: Kingsferry Building Society is refurbishing 14 branches and launching a mobile savings app. Project manager Rhys Pritchard plans the branch works linear-sequentially: designs are fixed, priced and then built. The app is developed iteratively, with the product backlog reprioritized after each user review. The project is hybrid. It still has an initiation stage, delivery stages with end stage decisions by the project board, and a business case checked at each boundary.

teach.text: Iterative does not mean unmanaged. An iterative-incremental project under PRINCE2 still has an initiation stage, management stages, tolerances and a business case. Delivery approach changes how products are built; it does not switch off any principle.

items: Three delivery approaches: linear-sequential, iterative-incremental, hybrid (1.5.3).
Linear-sequential: steps follow each other; products defined in detail up front.
Iterative-incremental: products evolve in cycles; criteria refined alongside development using a product backlog; may use several delivery stages.
Hybrid: a mix, such as linear for infrastructure and iterative for software.
PRINCE2 governs any approach without changing its principles; minimum two stages (initiation plus delivery).

summary: You can now define linear-sequential, iterative-incremental and hybrid delivery, and say which suits a given piece of work. You can also explain that PRINCE2 governs any of them with the same principles and at least two stages.

A.q: Which delivery approach has steps following one after another, with products defined in detail up front?
options: Linear-sequential
Iterative-incremental
Hybrid
Product-based
A.why: In a linear-sequential approach, steps such as design, build and test follow each other, and product descriptions are detailed enough to estimate with confidence before building.

whyNot.1: Iterative-incremental products evolve through repeated cycles rather than being fully defined up front.
whyNot.2: Hybrid mixes approaches; the description given is purely linear-sequential.
whyNot.3: Product-based planning is a PRINCE2 planning technique, not one of the three delivery approaches.

A.q: In an iterative-incremental approach, how are quality and acceptance criteria handled?
options: Fixed in full during starting up a project
Agreed by the supplier after each handover
Refined alongside development using a product backlog
Set by the business layer at the end of the project
A.why: In iterative-incremental delivery, quality and acceptance criteria are refined in parallel with development, using a product backlog.

whyNot.0: Fixing all criteria up front is typical of linear-sequential delivery, not iterative-incremental.
whyNot.1: Criteria are refined during development, with users involved, not agreed by the supplier after handover.
whyNot.3: Criteria guide development as it happens; they are not set by the business layer at the end.

A.q: What is a hybrid delivery approach?
options: Using internal and external suppliers on the same project
Running two linear-sequential projects side by side
Delivering iteratively with fixed scope and fixed budget
Mixing linear and iterative delivery for different parts
A.why: A hybrid approach mixes the two, for example linear-sequential for infrastructure and iterative-incremental for software.

whyNot.0: Using internal and external suppliers is a commercial arrangement, not a delivery approach.
whyNot.1: Two linear-sequential projects are still linear-sequential, not a mix of approaches.
whyNot.2: Fixing scope and budget does not make delivery hybrid; hybrid means mixing linear and iterative delivery.

B.q: Identify the missing word in the following sentence. A simple project with few, well-understood products and a mature delivery method may need just [?] stages: initiation and one delivery stage.
options: one
two
three
four
B.why: A simple project may need just two stages: the initiation stage and one delivery stage, which is also the PRINCE2 minimum.

whyNot.0: A PRINCE2 project has at least two stages, because initiation is always a stage of its own.
whyNot.2: Three stages would mean two delivery stages; the simple case described needs just one.
whyNot.3: Four stages is more than the simple case needs; initiation plus one delivery stage is enough.

B.q: Which statement about PRINCE2 and delivery approaches is correct?
options: PRINCE2 requires linear-sequential delivery to fit its stages
PRINCE2 replaces its processes with sprints in iterative work
PRINCE2 governs any approach without changing its principles
PRINCE2 drops the initiation stage when work is iterative
B.why: PRINCE2 is not specific to any delivery method: it can govern linear, iterative or hybrid delivery, and all seven principles still apply.

whyNot.0: PRINCE2 is not tied to linear-sequential delivery; stages are management stages, not delivery steps.
whyNot.1: PRINCE2's processes still govern the project; iterative cycles happen within its delivery stages.
whyNot.3: Every PRINCE2 project has an initiation stage, whatever the delivery approach.

B.q: Product descriptions detailed enough to estimate cost and time with confidence before building starts are typical of which delivery approach?
options: Iterative-incremental
Linear-sequential
Hybrid
Incremental release
B.why: Linear-sequential delivery defines products in detail up front, so product descriptions support confident cost and time estimates.

whyNot.0: In iterative-incremental delivery, products and criteria evolve, so detail is not all available up front.
whyNot.2: Hybrid mixes approaches; the full up-front detail described is characteristic of linear-sequential.
whyNot.3: Incremental release is part of iterative-incremental delivery, not a separate approach with full up-front detail.

C.q:
Which two statements about delivery approaches are correct?
1. An iterative-incremental project may have several delivery stages.
2. Linear-sequential delivery refines acceptance criteria during development using a backlog.
3. A hybrid approach can combine linear and iterative work in one project.
4. An iterative-incremental project does not need an initiation stage.
options: 1 and 2
2 and 4
3 and 4
1 and 3
C.why: Iterative projects may use several delivery stages (statement 1), and hybrid combines linear and iterative work (statement 3).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is false: refining criteria alongside development with a backlog describes iterative-incremental delivery.
whyNot.1: Statements 2 and 4 are false: statement 2 describes iterative delivery, and every PRINCE2 project has an initiation stage.
whyNot.2: Statement 4 is false: an initiation stage is needed whatever the delivery approach.

C.q: A housing developer's groundworks have stable, well-understood requirements, while its residents' app will evolve with user feedback. Which approach suits the project overall, and why?
options: Linear-sequential, because the groundworks carry most of the cost
Hybrid, because parts suit linear and parts suit iterative delivery
Iterative-incremental, because the app depends on user feedback
Linear-sequential, because PRINCE2 stages must run in sequence
C.why: Stable groundworks suit linear-sequential delivery and the evolving app suits iterative-incremental, so the project as a whole is hybrid.

whyNot.0: Cost share does not decide the approach; the app's evolving needs suit iterative delivery.
whyNot.2: The app suits iterative delivery, but the stable groundworks suit linear delivery, so the whole is hybrid.
whyNot.3: Management stages run in sequence, but that does not force linear-sequential delivery of products.

C.q: A bank's project uses iterative-incremental delivery from a product backlog. What still applies from PRINCE2, and how might its stages look?
options: All seven principles; several delivery stages after initiation
All seven principles; a single stage merging initiation and delivery
Four of the principles; several delivery stages after initiation
The processes but not the principles; one stage for every sprint
C.why: All seven principles apply whatever the approach, and an iterative project may run several delivery stages after the initiation stage.

whyNot.1: Initiation is always a separate stage, so delivery cannot be merged into it.
whyNot.2: All seven principles must be applied for a project to be PRINCE2; there is no partial set.
whyNot.3: The principles always apply, and PRINCE2 does not require one management stage per sprint.

reteach.title: Think of cooking a meal
reteach.question: Baking a wedding cake to a fixed recipe is different from making a curry and tasting as you go. How do these map to delivery approaches?

blocks.h: Recipe or tasting as you go
blocks.body: A wedding cake follows a fixed recipe: measure, mix, bake, ice, in that order. That is linear-sequential. A curry is cooked by tasting and adjusting in rounds until it is right. That is iterative-incremental. A dinner party with a fixed-recipe cake and a taste-as-you-go curry is hybrid. Whichever you choose, the host still decides the menu, the budget and when to call it done: that is PRINCE2's governance.

blocks.text: The host's control (budget, decision points, when to stop) stays the same for both dishes, just as PRINCE2's principles stay the same for every delivery approach.

explain.body: Steps follow each other (for example design, build, test). Products are defined in detail up front, with product descriptions detailed enough to estimate cost and time with confidence.

options: Products evolve through repeated review cycles
Products are defined in detail before building
Criteria are refined using a product backlog
Work mixes cycles and steps for different parts
test.why: Linear-sequential delivery defines products in detail up front, and the steps then follow each other.

whyNot.0: Products evolving through cycles is iterative-incremental delivery.
whyNot.2: Refining criteria with a product backlog is iterative-incremental delivery.
whyNot.3: Mixing approaches for different parts is hybrid delivery.

explain.body: Products evolve through repeated cycles. Quality and acceptance criteria are refined in parallel with development using a product backlog, and the project may have several delivery stages.

test.q: In iterative-incremental delivery, what is used to refine requirements and criteria as development proceeds?
options: Product flow diagram
Product backlog
Risk register
Work breakdown structure
test.why: Iterative-incremental delivery refines quality and acceptance criteria in parallel with development, using a product backlog.

whyNot.0: A product flow diagram shows the sequence and dependencies of products in planning; it is not the backlog.
whyNot.2: The risk register records risks, not evolving requirements.
whyNot.3: A work breakdown structure is a hierarchy of all the work; it is not used to refine criteria during development.

explain.body: A mix of linear-sequential and iterative-incremental delivery in one project, for example linear for infrastructure and iterative for software.

test.q: A project builds a new depot to a fixed design and develops its scheduling software in increments. Which delivery approach is this?
options: Linear-sequential
Iterative-incremental
Hybrid
Commercial
test.why: A fixed-design building (linear) plus incrementally developed software (iterative) in one project is a hybrid approach.

whyNot.0: The building is linear-sequential, but the software is iterative, so the whole is hybrid.
whyNot.1: The software is iterative, but the fixed-design building is linear, so the whole is hybrid.
whyNot.3: Commercial describes a customer and supplier context, not a delivery approach.

explain.body: PRINCE2 is not specific to any delivery method. All seven principles apply, and every project has at least two stages: initiation plus one or more delivery stages.

test.q: Whatever the delivery approach, what is the minimum number of stages in a PRINCE2 project?
options: One: a combined initiation and delivery stage
Three: initiation, delivery and closing stages
Two: initiation and at least one delivery stage
Four: one each for design, build, test and close
test.why: Every PRINCE2 project has at least two stages: the initiation stage and at least one delivery stage.

whyNot.0: Initiation is always a stage in its own right, so there cannot be just one combined stage.
whyNot.1: Closing a project happens within the final delivery stage; it is not a stage of its own.
whyNot.3: Design, build and test are delivery steps, not required management stages.
